question: In question E-002344-191, I spoke out against the fact that, in Italy, EU agricultural funds are one of the main sources of income in the mafia’s economic strategy, and are also being used to finance mafia bosses who are fugitives from justice. An investigative report published in February 20242 analysed the open source database farmsubsidy.

org3 and found that family members of mafia boss Matteo Messina Denaro were among the CAP subsidy beneficiaries. The news story highlights the systematic problems the institutions face in stopping the mafia feeding off CAP funds, given the absence of anti-mafia checks for sums below EUR 25 000.

Furthermore, the fact that journalists have to resort to using an open source database highlights the lack of official information on CAP beneficiaries in Italy, undermining EU efforts to be transparent towards European taxpayers. Can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Will the Commission check whether further CAP funding has fallen into the hands of relatives and associates of Matteo Messina Denaro and, based on the information in its possession, state how much CAP funding has now ended up with Cosa Nostra?
What specific provisions, based on the Antoci Protocol, has it adopted to stop the financing of the mafia through the CAP in Europe?
How does it view the minimum threshold of EUR 25 000 for anti-mafia checks and the lack of transparency concerning small amounts (E-001095/2017(ASW))4?
answer: The rules on ex-post publication of beneficiaries under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) are contained in Regulation (EU) 2021/2116 (1) of the European Parliament and of the Council (Articles 98-100) and Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/128 (Articles 58-62). Member States publish the names of the beneficiaries on the Internet, and the Member States’ websites are then published by the Commission (2).

Concerning, the beneficiaries of small amounts, the choice of the co-legislators was to set a threshold of EUR 1,250 below which the name of the beneficiary should not be published. This rule is justified by the need to strike a balance between the right of the public to know how EU funds are spent and the right of individuals to protect their personal data.

The Directorate General for Agriculture and Rural Development of the Commission has issued a note to the Member States, based on judgments of the Court of Justice (3), to clarify that the land for which CAP funding is claimed should be at the farmer’s disposal in a lawful way and in accordance with applicable national law.

In addition, the Member States have the right to require appropriate proof of the actual and lawful land use and have a general obligation to carry out systematic checks to prevent and correct irregularities.

The minimum threshold of EUR 25,000 for anti-mafia checks, referred to by the Honourable Member, is an established national rule, aimed at improving the effectiveness of controls to prevent and tackle irregularities and fraud affecting, inter alia, the Union budget with respect to funds the management of which is entrusted to the competent national authorities, and it is under the sole responsibility of the Member State in question.
